author: ValWood
body:
I'm picking up a 

GO:0004835 | tubulin-tyrosine ligase activity | IEA with 17605

for https://www.pombase.org/gene/SPAC12B10.04

but I am not convinced that yeast have this modification.

Claude says:
No. Budding yeast (S. cerevisiae) don't run the tyrosination/detyrosination cycle. They have no tubulin tyrosine ligase (TTL) gene, so nothing can add a tyrosine back to α-tubulin.
What their α-tubulin ends in: The main α-tubulin, Tub1, ends in phenylalanine (…EEF), not tyrosine. That aromatic last residue makes it chemically similar to "tyrosinated" tubulin, and it stays in that state all the time.
No detyrosination either: Yeast don't appear to have the enzymes that remove the last residue in animal cells (vasohibins/SVBP, MATCAP). So "Glu-tubulin" doesn't form naturally.

So.....

1. I checked and I cant find any evidence of detyrosinases.

2. Badin-Larçon et al. (PNAS 2004) engineered yeast whose Tub1 lacks the final Phe, mimicking Glu-tubulin. ....so I assume the absence was established here.

3. More broadly, yeast tubulins carry fewer of the C-terminal modifications seen in animals (polyglutamylation, polyglycylation, and so on). See this ticket too https://github.com/geneontology/go-ontology/issues/33005

4. SGD annotates PBY1 (YBR094W) as a putative tubulin tyrosine ligase associated with P-bodies, with a possible role in mRNA metabolism. Sweet et al. (RNA, 2007) BUT the organization is a bit differnet Pby1 is a 753-residue protein. Its N-terminus (MRVLITNDDG…) looks like a SurE-type phosphatase/nucleotidase motif, fused to the TTL-like ATP-grasp domain.

5. TTL-fold enzymes catalyse many ligation reactions (glutamylation, glycylation, and others), and not all of them act on tubulin. 

On balance it seems that this  propagation is probalby not sound, or at least requires  more evidence.
title: GO:0004835	 tubulin-tyrosine ligase activity IEA with 17605 (rhea)
